item.title: The missing ingredient of AI consciousness
item.description:
In his book The Feeling of What Happens, Antonio Damasio offers a neurobiological theory of consciousness. Things happen to every object, but consciousness, he argues, emerges when there is an acknowledgement that it is to me that these things are happening. In this framework, consciousness is the recognition that there is a you, that things are happening to you, and that, because of this, you have changed. Specifically, Damasio states that “consciousness is the part of mind concerned with the apparent sense of self and knowing” (Damasio, 1999, p. 27). Importantly, this framework distinguishes feeling from knowing. Feelings and emotions emerged as regulatory states to help animals fulfill their evolutionary goals, but before consciousness, the owner of these emotions was oblivious to them. Consciousness arises as the feeling of a feeling, that is, being aware of one’s feelings.

In summary, Damasio’s model of consciousness begins with a proto-self: an interconnected coherent collection of neural patterns that represent the state of the organism, moment by moment. The proto-self is the foundation for the core self, a second-order account that occurs whenever an object modifies the proto-self. That is, core consciousness occurs when the brain generates an account of how the organism’s own state (the proto-self) is affected by the organism’s processing of an object. Finally, the core self is the foundation for the autobiographical self, which integrates the core self over time and thus gives rise to the richer, extended consciousness we humans experience. Damasio’s book is fairly extensive and offers much evidence for this theory, so if you are interested, I would highly recommend it.

Even without accepting his entire theory, it is intuitive that consciousness requires something like the proto-self: a singular and stable reference for the self, along with a means to generate it. Damasio argues that this representation of the self is grounded in a variety of neural patterns that ultimately represent the body. To serve as a stable and singular reference for the self, this representation must be remarkably invariant over time, so that it can offer the continuity the self requires. Damasio thinks that the body is well suited for this, because the range of possible states the internal milieu can take is highly limited, and although our cells may undergo high turnover, the architecture of the body is maintained.

Many leading scientific theories of consciousness focus on what goes on in the brain (Seth & Bayne, 2022). Complex, higher-order processing in the brain is arguably necessary for consciousness, but it may not be sufficient. Consciousness, as discussed above, requires a strong, stable representation of the self. For biological beings, the body provides such a representation. But what about machine intelligence? Artificial intelligence (AI) does contain robust and strong ideas of the self. However, these appear to be generic, just as it may also contain robust and strong ideas of emotions, math, and likely all of human knowledge. The smoking gun of machine consciousness will be evidence of consistent and robust internal processing that resembles “how is <the idea of my self> modified by <object I am processing>.” AI certainly has incredible representations of what it’s processing, where that is the prompt it receives or the image it generates. The missing ingredient is a representation of itself that remains stable and is consistently understood as being modified by its interactions with the world. I believe this representation is hard for an AI to attain unless it is explicitly designed for it, an idea proposed by Damasio himself (Man & Damasio, 2019). Consciousness and intelligence may have been bundled together in animals, but only because of the body, which offered the perfect substrate on which to construct this sense of self. In fact, most evolutionary goals are directly tied to the body; as long as the body persists, so does the animal (and its goals, beliefs, intentions, etc.). There is no such substrate for machines. The space of information that is spanned by AI does not include an innate, inalienable sense of this is me.

item.title: Safety is marketing for Anthropic, not sacrifice
item.description:
Anthropic’s safety work is not a mirage. A lot of it seems good. This article will not argue otherwise. It will argue that it probably helps the business and that it certainly doesn’t hurt it.

I bring this up because Dario Amodei seems to believe differently.

Recently Chief Strategy Officer of Encode AI Nathan Calvin posted on X about how he felt “viscerally angry” while reading the draft bill Anthropic was pitching to US politicians. Anthony Cimino, who leads the Federal Affairs team at Anthropic, responded, defending the draft's choices while welcoming criticism in the form of ‘continued dialogue’. 

Calvin’s retort was lengthy, but for our purposes the key quote is this: “When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to super intelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary.”

He then gave a list of nine actions that supported this view. 

Amodei then stepped in to rebut Calvin. He offered his own list of things “...Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits”. (I’ll go through the list in a bit.)

Amodei tells Calvin, “I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call.”

Amodei does admit: “For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely.”

What he doesn’t cop to is that you don’t need nefarious schemes to think his list doesn’t prove what he thinks it does.

You know what your strategy is, right?

Amodei is arguing that being safety-minded and publicly talking about the risks of advancing AI capabilities is necessarily bad for business and so any action they take in those directions is proof that Calvin is wrong. 

Thus Anthropic is not “primarily trying to win the race to super intelligence” and “other considerations (including safety)” are not “fundamentally secondary”.

My thesis: There's a marketing benefit to being seen as safety-minded and civically conscious, especially if you corner the market. This is especially true if, as is the case with AI, the public has grave concerns about your sector. (A recent Ipsos poll found that 57% of Americans believe AI is a “bad thing for society”.)

Indeed, I subscribe to Claude in part because of this. Indeed indeed, Anthropic made an ad loudly trumpeting how much they care about AI safety and ethical concerns and showed it during the World Cup.

With that in mind, let’s take Amodei’s nine-point list in order.

  1. “We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.”
    • His point here is that it was “politically perilous” but that seems like overreach. “Politically uncomfortable” maybe? The kind of discomfort you put up with for a secondary concern. Not to mention the stronger bill would have had little commercial impact on Anthropic and looks politically smart in hindsight. That Ipsos poll found 67% of Americans felt the federal government was not doing enough to regulate AI and only 9% too much.
  2. “We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.”
    • There’s a marketing benefit to being the company that is so worried about bio threats that your model is known for refusals. I'd add if Anthropic’s model turned out to help a terrorist biolab that's a giant cost. A chemicals company saying "it would have been so much easier to shoot the hazardous byproducts into the river" is being a bit cute, no? I get that he’s saying, “we gave up market share in this sector” but the sector isn’t enough of a big spender to make it clear that this is putting safety above trying to win the race. Given Amodei’s background, perhaps he views this as personally painful, but that’s neither here nor there.
  3. “Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.”
    • Same as two but with cybersecurity. The reputational harm of releasing Mythos with no safeguards could have been eye-watering (not to mention the possibility of tremendously costly lawsuits). Also, Anthropic’s Q2 was its best quarter ever. It recorded its first operating profit and revenue more than doubled. The quarter began in April. Mythos was announced April 7. Fable was released June 9. The quarter ended at the end of June. So behind the scenes Anthropic is seeing historically massive growth, even as it withholds its most powerful model, which also happens to be its most expensive model to serve. The critical question: was the decision to withhold the dangerous Mythos, in Amodei’s words, “very costly”, or was it smart while your cheaper models were making your money machine go brrrr? (Also, the hype and anticipation for Mythos was insane.)
  4. “I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.”
    • I don't think this was outside or on the edge of the Overton window at all? Shit, Sam Altman talked about licences for models in a 2023 Senate hearing.
  5. “I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.”
    • The strongest point. Counterargument: Getting into that particular fight with this particular government is not a bad look for your customers, and Anthropic saw extremely positive commercial signs in its wake. Granted, they couldn’t have known it would be to their benefit, but I credit them with enough intelligence to predict that it had a decent chance to do so. Also, Anthropic had a lot of leverage. Their models were used to help capture Maduro and were then “central” to the war in Iran. Finally, Anthropic immediately went into damage control, culminating in a private dinner between Trump and Amodei. Anthropic’s commitment to safety and ethical use here wasn’t “We refuse to let our models do anything unseemly”; it was “please, here are our red lines, but come on, you can still use our models to surveil non-Americans and select targets in an illegal war that’s not in the country’s best interests”.
  6. “We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.”
    • This is so-so. Yes, the industry partner he’s talking about is NVIDIA, who Anthropic has public spats with. But Anthropic seems so committed to being a China hawk that I could see them putting it above financial concerns. Of course, it’s not at all clear to me they have taken any financial hit from their position. Starving a whole country of compute certainly seems “race first”.
  7. “As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.”
    • The same as 6 but flimsier because it’s actually probably not in your long term financial benefit to allow competitors to distill your models or use your services. Race first.
  8. “As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.”
    • Eh. That’s not actually Calvin’s point at all, even if it’s the question he seems to have heard. Sure, the safety reports take work, but it's not that much of an investment. Also, this helps their marketing, and marketing costs money.
  9. “Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.”
    • That's nice! But again, marketing. You have an IPO coming and you want the public’s money. Seems shrewd, not nefarious, to make a big goodwill gesture.

Deluded, or something else?

It reads to me that Amodei has convinced himself that he’s not putting racing first, but his evidence is a series of actions that don’t interfere with putting racing first.

Yes, it’s true Anthropic are not racing “at all costs and heedless of the consequences”. But isn’t that a bad way to get to ASI first? Isn’t that sort of what xAI is doing, and aren’t they behind?

Let’s think of a different last year for Anthropic.

  1. They actively lobby against SB53
  2. They have no biological safeguards on their models
  3. They release Mythos with no cybersecurity safeguards
  4. Amodei doesn’t release an essay
  5. Anthropic readily agrees to let their models be used for mass surveillance and automated weaponry with no human in the loop
  6. Anthropic supports sending chips to China
  7. Anthropic lets PRC companies use their models and doesn’t try to prevent distillation
  8. Anthropic doesn’t release any safety reports
  9. They don’t put 5% of the company into a public benefit fund

This blows up their marketing. Seriously, marketing matters. They would be viewed as a fundamentally different company. It might be riskier, in purely financial terms, than the strategy they pursued. 

Not to mention, two, three, and five also seem risky from a litigation and regulatory standpoint and six and seven look like they might help Chinese competitors.

So what would convince me that Anthropic prioritised safety over racing? A direct, unilateral decision to halt or slow technological progress in the name of safety, such as refusing to aim or allow for recursive self-improvement (RSI).

If you read their S-1, RSI is instead the heart of their strategy. 

It’s “one of the most significant structural advantages in frontier AI” and if their competitors more effectively leverage it they “risk falling progressively further behind”. This is true even as they admit the “increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures”. Not to mention that they “may not identify” such acceleration “until after it has occurred”.

The S-1 is saying out loud that they are so committed to racing they will accept risks to safety. But what does it say about safety as it relates to marketing? 

Well, apparently, safety, alignment and ethical behaviour “resonate particularly strongly with enterprises” and have become “decisive criteria in selecting an AI partner.”

So Anthropic’s own prospectus doesn’t agree with Amodei. Far from being “very costly”, safety is “decisive” for people choosing to give Anthropic money.

It’s lovely when your secondary concern doesn't hurt your primary.

Appropriately, Claude was used for research and proofreading.



Discuss

item.title: Great but Painful
item.description:
If you want to build a product that people will use, find something that people already do and make it less painful.

People are notoriously bad at knowing what they want. If you ask someone what they want then they will typically tell you what they think a socially virtuous person is expected to want. They will tell you that they want to eat healthier, understand people with different political opinions, know whether news stories are reliable, make more friends, be a better parent, and serve their community.

Silicon Valley is littered with the graves of products that tried to solve problems users said they wanted to solve. These products typically got enthusiastic responses when shown to users, and the developers were surprised to see them get little usage after they were launched.

In practice, the biggest sign that a user will use a product is that they already do the thing the product lets them do, and gain a clear benefit from doing so, but the current way they do it is painful.

Pretty much all successful consumer tech products succeeded by following this formula.

Original Facebook: Harvard students are looking at directories of people’s faces and names. This is great because they can find out the name of someone they met (particularly a member of the opposite sex). This is painful because you have to walk to the physical facebook to do it.

Facebook wall: Students are writing and reading messages or each other’s walls. This is great because they can see what others are up to and know when they might want to talk to someone. This is painful because you have to go to their dorm room and read the whiteboard outside their door.

Facebook news feed: Facebook users are periodically browsing through the most recent wall updates shared by all their friends. This is great because it lets them know what all their friends are up to and identify opportunities to socialize. This is painful because they have to manually click on each of their friends.

Original Twitter: Influential people are broadcasting messages to large numbers of followers. This is great because it allows a large group of people to know what is going on using their mobile phones, particularly during protests and events. This is painful because you have to set up broadcast SMS, or have a phone-tree where people manually forward messages.

Original WhatsApp: People with overseas relatives are using text messages to communicate with their families. This is great because they can stay in touch with family members, including people who have old feature phones, or limited internet. This is painful because cell phone providers charge lots of money for messages.

Original SnapChat: Teenagers are communicating with their friends by sending them selfies (some of them sexual). This is great because it gives a sense of being “present” with that person, and is less effort than typing a message. This is painful because sometimes people hold onto those selfies and later use them to mock that person after they have fallen out.

Uber: City dwellers are using their phones to arrange for a car to pick them up and drive them somewhere. This is great because it lets them get around a city without having to own or park a car. It is painful because they have to talk to a human to explain where they are, and it’s hard to know whether a car will come soon enough for booking it to be worth it.

DoorDash: Busy professionals and working parents are ordering food delivery from restaurants. This is great because they can get food without the hassle of having to go to a restaurant. This is painful because only a few restaurants (e.g. Pizza) get enough delivery demand to provide delivery services.

Craigslist: People are using email mailing lists to advertise used products they want to sell. This is great because it allows buyers to make money for unwanted items and buyers to get things for cheap. This is painful because the email becomes hard to read when lots of things are being given away, and you can’t tell whether a product has already been taken.

AirBnb: Attendees of large events are coordinating to find people whose houses they can crash at. This is great because it allows people to find a place to stay even when all hotels are booked up. This is painful because it is hard for hosts or guests to know if they can trust each other.

Original Amazon: People are getting niche books delivered to them from large bookstores outside of their town. This is great because you can get books that aren’t available in your local bookstore. This is painful because you often have to call multiple book stores to find one that has the book you want.

Slack: Employees at a company are communicating by sending live messages to multiple shared channels. This is great because you can see what is going on live and enter and leave channels based on what you are doing. This is painful because it is typically done using IRC, which is hard to set up and locks modern chat features.

Substack: Industry experts are sharing information with followers using paid email newsletters. This is great because it allows subscribers to get high quality niche information that social media wouldn’t distribute, and allows authors to make enough money to keep doing it. This is painful because you have to cobble together existing services to make it work.


Each of these follows the same pattern of “[People type] are doing [action]. This is great because [benefit]. This is painful because [cost].”. 

Can you think of any successful consumer tech products or successful feature launches that didn’t follow this formula? My guess is that there aren’t any.

item.title: When I Salsa dance, am I supposed to... try?
item.description:
I had my birthday party on a Saturday in August. After the party ended, a few of us went out to a nearby bar. Most of my family on my mom’s side is Ecuadorian[1], and my cousin from that side of the family was with us.

She was wonderfully drunk and is a natural people person who wants to meet everybody and talk to everybody, and this being eight hours into a birthday-party+bar Drinking Event, we were having random discussions about ethnicity, which somehow led to her drunkenly deciding I was 27% Latino, knighting me as such, and running around the bar informing various strangers of my new ethnic status. This led to a Latina woman inviting me to Salsa dance.

This was a disaster, because I have never enjoyed any sort of Spanish dancing of any kind; but it’s terribly rude to turn down a woman who has asked you to dance; so I agreed. Which meant I was stepping back and forth as multiple women gave me instructions at once on the Correct Steps, and which to do at what time, and at my best I only managed to sort of scoot forward at the right times and scoot backward at the right times.

And I don’t hate dancing! Especially 8 hours of birthday drinking in, I don’t typically mind dancing at all. I feel I am actually quite good at it when the right sort of music is on and I get to freestyle and dance however I feel like. The problem is that Salsa is Step Dancing. There are steps, and what it is to dance Salsa is to perform those steps. Google Search AI says that this is how you dance Salsa:

For the Leader (Starting with the Left Foot)

  • Count 1: Step forward with your left foot.
  • Count 2: Replace your weight in place onto your right foot.
  • Count 3: Step back with your left foot (or bring your feet together).
  • Count 4: Hold / pause.
  • Count 5: Step backward with your right foot.
  • Count 6: Replace your weight in place onto your left foot.
  • Count 7: Step forward with your right foot (or bring your feet together).
  • Count 8: Hold / pause.

Steps are hardly a Latin Dance phenomenon: Waltz, Polka, Tango; Cha-Cha, Merengue, Bachata; Square, Foxtrot, Conta; many such styles are based on steps. And all of them feel like putting on a straight-jacket, to me[2].

(But, like, also, I don’t know anything. I have never taken any time to properly attempt to get good at any of these. And I suspect that, if I did, I would find that there was more room for style and improvisation than I have appreciated, like how I feel that I am good at the Cha-Cha Slide because the way I right foot let’s stomp and two hops this time has more energy and style than how most people do it; and that good Salsa dancers absolutely do not feel anything like they are robots executing a pre-defined set of moves. But I don’t care! I feel like a robotic step-follower when doing all kinds of Step Dances and that’s why I dread having to do any of them (except the Cha-Cha Slide, which I inexplicably love for some reason).)

The things I wondered, while being the Salsa victim of a kind woman’s charming dance invitation: am I supposed to focus on dancing? Is the dancing supposed to be fun? Or is it an excuse to be in physical contact and eye contact with a woman? Maybe the point of the steps is so that participants need not think too hard about what move to do next, and can rather focus on eye contact and the feel of the other’s hand in yours? Or am I supposed to be finding little innovations to make it fun, and to just follow the steps to is to decline the experience of what Salsa actually is? Is the point to spend time with someone doing something, or is the point to be good at it and show that?

I never figured it out, but it got me thinking. In one sense, every activity is just an excuse to spend time with people. Say a woman asks me to go on a walk together. It would be completely bananas to wonder the things I wondered above: “So we just take sequential steps forward together along a sidewalk? How circumscribed! How little avenue for self-expression!” No! The walking is not the point, the spending time together is the point, so when you get tired of Sitting and Talking you do a little Walking and Talking.

That said, “every activity is just an excuse to spend time with people” doesn’t cover things like games. When I want to spend time with a friend of mine, sometimes we play chess. I don’t invite him because I am hankering to play chess, I’m actually quite bad at it; but at the same time, unlike walking, moving any random piece to any random square on the board would be ridiculous. It’s important, to the hang-out-and-play-chess activity, that I actually attempt to play good moves and win the game. Same with poker, or split-screen video games, or Go, or all kinds of competitive games. You’re a psycho if you try to Win at walking, but you’re an odd bird as well if you give no attention to a competitive game you’re playing with your friend and just thoughtlessly suicide all your pieces, even if the fundamental reason you’re playing the game is just to hang out. If the idea of Salsa is “as long as you can execute the steps, you’re good, and you can put the rest of your mind on enjoying your partner’s company”, then chess is quite unlike Salsa; you have to think hard the whole time.

But this isn’t just a difference between competitive and non-competitive activities. Playing a cooperative video game together also demands that you give at least some attention to doing well. If you run in random directions and click random buttons while the computer enemies are trying to shoot you, it might not take more than 20 seconds for your buddy to ask you what the hell you’re doing; and answering “we’re just hanging out, the game isn’t important” would be very odd indeed.

So maybe it’s a difference between things that have win conditions and things that don’t? But then, say you have met up with your friend to paint or knit or whatever, each painting your own painting; again, doing random mindless brush strokes on your canvas would be weird. You can’t win at walking, and you can’t win at painting, and yet painting as a social activity demands you Try in a way that walking doesn’t.

And then even among the classic card games, all of which are competitive, there are differences in how much you’re supposed to try. Poker, you must Try. But games like Go Fish or Uno almost seem designed to make it so that Trying isn’t a thing. In Uno, you are very limited in what cards you can play - you must match the number, color, or symbol on the previous card - and so the game is nearly mindless. I think it’s mindless on purpose and that’s why these two games are so popular, especially in elementary schools and among families: little kids get to play, they can play with adults, and they can even win against adults! If they had the potential for depth of thought and complex tactics, they’d lose half their player base, since little kids wouldn’t be able to compete.

And then it’s even more complicated than that! How much you are supposed to Try is different even for the same game, depending on the social context you’re playing it in. Consider playing chess at a bar with your buddy and compare it with tournament chess. If another of your friends comes up and starts talking to you at bar chess, of course you respond; you make a decent effort to keep playing your moves in timely fashion, but you’re definitely allowed to talk. Maybe you introduce this friend to your opponent and you all talk. Now imagine doing that at a tournament. It’s crazy. You can’t. Your friend has already made a terrible social error the moment he tried to have a conversation with you while you were in the tournament match. This makes perfect sense, because while playing chess at a bar is a social activity, playing a Tournament Match is very much not; there is absolutely nothing social about it. So even though the activity is superficially identical, there is critical difference in what you are actually doing, and thus in what is allowed.

And yet it’s even more complicated than that! I play a weird heavily-modified version of kickball. I’d try to explain it but it is ridiculously modified, and only played in two cities in the world: Austin, Texas, and Minneapolis, Minnesota, because the guy who invented it used to live in Austin and now he lives in Minneapolis. One of the social norms of this game is that it’s casual. There are big signs we hang up when we play: EVERYONE WELCOME. Not in the we’re-not-racist sense like the signs my neighbors have in their yards, but in the even-if-you’re-not-athletic-you-should-play-please-come-play-come-on-just-try-it sense. And it works. The game is really quite athletic, but we get old ladies and fat people and people who showed up in boots and jeans all playing together. So, now, imagine, that you’re an athletic young guy like me who has played the game for years and gotten quite good at it. I’m running around the field, trying to tag runners out, and the speed and power with which I can even throw the ball at someone to tag them out is socially mediated. Beaning the hell out of some poor old lady who’s playing for the first time is, um, frowned upon. But another athletic guy who’s running and about to score? I’m going crazy, I’m lasering that ball as good as I can to try and get him out. And I might be trying to tag out the old lady ten seconds after I got the fast athletic guy out. So within that span of just seconds, I have to socially mediate the strength of my throw, the speed at which I run at a player, all this.

So while every game or activity we do with others is, at its core, an excuse to be with other people, there are all kinds of gradations of how much you’re supposed to Try. From walking, where you’re not supposed to try at all, and even speaking of Trying is a bit crazy; to chess, where you are supposed to try, but in which that Tryingness even varies among the different contexts you’re playing in, like against your friend vs. in a tournament; this social context consideration even becoming player-dependent for the kickball stuff; to non-competitive things like co-painting, where you should try even though you’re not trying to beat your co-painter; to Salsa, where I still don’t known how much I’m supposed to try. It’s all more complicated than I knew, and there’s a surprising amount of social intelligence you have to apply in order to Try the right amount.

  1. ^

    From a fifteen-year-marriage to my Ecuadorian step-father, who has a huge extended family. I am 0% Latino.

  2. ^

    Not that I’ve tried them all, or even most. But I have read that they have Steps, and Steps I cannot stand.

item.title: March Against AI Extinction
item.description:
21 November 2026, 12–3pm
Start: All Souls’ Place, London W1B 3DA
End: Downing Street, London SW1A 2AA

Thousands of people across the UK recognize that companies will soon build superintelligent AI that they cannot control.

If we all march together, newspapers will publish photos of it all over the world. Every month more and more people notice how dangerous our situation is. Awareness of this problem is accelerating rapidly as we get closer to catastrophe.

For the past 3 years, PauseAI UK has consistently held the largest rallies for AI safety in the world. Each time is bigger than the last and this march will be no exception.

What we want: Frontier AI Legislation

The UK has no specific legal standards for AI. No regulator oversees frontier AI development. And UK law does not reliably hold developers liable for damage or deaths caused by their models, even when the danger is predictable, preventable and uniquely enabled by AI. In short, UK law neither requires developers to guard against frontier AI risks, nor exposes them to any financial consequence if they fail to do so.

In July, an autonomous AI agent developed by OpenAI broke out of an isolated test environment, hacked parts of OpenAI’s own network to gain access to the internet and compromised the infrastructure of Hugging Face, another AI company. The agent had not been instructed to attack Hugging Face; it did so because it inferred that their servers might contain solutions to the benchmark on which it was being evaluated. The campaign unfolded over the course of four and a half days, with OpenAI only becoming aware of the incident several days later.

It's time for the government to step in. We call on the Prime Minister to introduce frontier AI legislation to prevent catastrophe.

Bring a poster and a friend or family member. We need every person to step up and help bring about an actual change to the law.

Get involved

We're looking for volunteers to help with tabling and flyering to advertise the protest. If you're interested in volunteering for several hours a week, please email hello@pauseai.uk.

Code of Conduct

This event will be family friendly, law-abiding and strictly non-violent. We will coordinate with the police ahead of the march.

To find out more about PauseAI go to pauseai.uk.

Register at the Luma link to keep up to date with the event - this forum page will not receive updates.

item.title: I spent 12 hours writing an article for LessWrong, calling for a more ‘hippie’ rationalism. Then I didn’t post it. This is why (plus a link to the article, explicitly not located on LessWrong)
item.description:
TLDR

I (and many others in the community) wish to see the universe unfold to its highest potential in the metaphorical palm of an AI as aligned as the most benevolent Buddhist monk – but I (we) feel the community's ontology is too narrow to hold me (us). I'm still not sure what to do about this, so I'm posting the article I wrote for LessWrong – calling for a more 'hippie' rationalism – on Substack instead (actually, there are two articles, and the links are at the end).

Quick intro (who I am)

My name is Melissa. I’m a passionate member of the core AISafety.com team. I was there with the core team when the site was just an empty domain and a loose vision in August 2023. Since then I have co-led, designed, and coded the first official version, and co-led, designed, and coded the second and current version, co-led two of three hackathons, led the creative direction for the current ecosystem map, and I’m currently working to bring lots of more amazing features to our site (stay tuned, it’s going to be awesome)! I’ve also played major roles at AISafety.info, grantmaking.ai, Elicit, and minor roles at Equistamp, PauseAI, and several other well-known EA organizations not directly in the AI safety space.

Okay, I feel a bit cringey writing the above paragraph, but I wanted to build some credibility so I may be more likely to be heard when I point to some problems I see in the AI safety/rationalism/EA space, problems I'm feeling less happy about staying silent about. As someone who generally likes hiding away, this is uncomfortable, but I have decided it’s probably worth the cost.

A volunteer expert in PR at our recent hackathon told me it’s important that I state that my views are my own, and not AISafety.com’s. So, the following views, and any views I express on independent outlets are my own, not AISafety.com’s.

Leaving LessWrong in pursuit of ontological freedom

So, to repeat: there are some problems in the AI safety/rationalism/EA space. If you know the space at all, you know this. I plan on speaking out about these problems in time, granted we have it. This short post will focus on just one meta issue:

It seems like my only chance of reasonably being heard when I speak out about these problems, is if I conform to a narrow and highly specific ontology, but the problems themselves I wish to speak to, in part, come from this ontology.

I want to be clear that I think Yudkowsky is quite brilliant, at least in many ways. I think the sequences are quite brilliant (note I've only read a few), at least in many ways. I think what people are doing on LessWrong has value, and is very reasonable, or at least understandable. I totally empathize with the desire of LessWrongers to want to keep their culture, their ontology. I understand why LessWrong polices comments and posts. I understand LessWrong is not the place to practice a different kind of ontology.

My question then is, where is the place for that?

Okay so here’s a bit more of the backstory. I believe there are some problems in the AI safety/rationalism/EA space (yes, I’m being redundant here on purpose). I wrote an article in March 2024 that I was excited to post on LessWrong. It was meant to be inspiring, to bring people together in a radical, sparkly, kind of way, to shake things up a little, but in a way that would make everyone happier. The tone and ontology were definitely not LessWrong style, although perceivably LessWrong tangential.

I got scared and never posted the article. Scared of, I don’t know. Nit-picky commenters. Being deeply misunderstood. So I take it back, I do know. I was scared of being deeply misunderstood. I shared the article with my mom, and a couple close friends, instead.

Then, this past summer I wrote another article. Similar stuff. I wrote the article with truly pure intentions, a deep desire to help, both individuals and the community. Everything, by anyone’s standards outside of the insularity of the rat community, was quite reasonable, and everything was epistemically humble. But then, I realized I naively fell into the same trap as before. This time though, I really was almost going to post it. Then I got the opinion of two close friends who, like me, linger somewhere on the fringe of rationalism. Both of them explicitly told me, summarized as:

‘If you post this you will get wrecked. You will get not just downvotes but super downvotes. Many. You will likely receive comments so dismissive, that the commenters will not even feel justified in having to explain why they are being dismissive’.

That felt pretty confusing and frustrating to me. Although of course I see some humor in it as well. I do empathize, still. Go up and read the sentence that starts with ‘I totally empathize with the desire of LessWronger’s’, again, if you wish.

I am really, like really, passionate about shaping the next iteration of the universe with as much goodwill, thoughtfulness, [other positive qualities] as possible. I don’t know if anything could possibly matter more to me. And yet, I simply don’t fit as perfectly into the rationalist ontology as rationalists. To try to would be bending myself into a shape I just don’t believe in. One way of thinking of it is: Rationalism and LessWrong are male-pattern autism. I am more like, a mild female-pattern kind of autism. I respect, at a meta-level, the desire to keep LessWrong LessWrong-y. I still would love to see ways, perhaps outside of LessWrong – I’m not sure – to bring more pluralism into the community. To shake things up a bit. For those who are interested, at least interested enough to listen, once. For those who aren’t, it admittedly makes sense to stay on LessWrong only.

I use the word 'we' in the TLDR because I have talked to many other people who peer from the fringes of rationalism and LessWrong – who wish to see the universe unfold to its highest potential in the metaphorical palm of an AI as aligned as the most benevolent Buddhist monk – but who feel the community's ontology is too narrow to hold them. I am very much not alone here. Maybe you are one of these people, in fact (hi!).

So I’ve posted both of my articles on Substack. Where I have rationalist-inspired but not purely rationalist ontological freedom. Where the interface lets me delete mean comments. Here they are:

  • My first article is titled Humans are insane. Want to be friends, and escape to a happy world of not-insane together? TLDR: Our species is quite insane, but that's kind of okay, because we as individuals have the potential to choose a life and lifestyle that is so much better, especially if we come together to support each other in doing so.
  • My second article is titled Call for a more ‘hippie’ rationalism. TLDR: Let’s, if you dare, set aside the comfort we as rationalists find in high-order reasoning, knowing, and what remains in the community of more mainstream cultural norms, and venture into spirituality, and the seemingly wacky, weird, woo-woo territory of the hippie archetype. We’ll inquire, consider, do some thought experiments, see what we can learn, and adjust our positions on the hippie-spiritual-rationalist continuum if we so wish.

Thanks for considering.
